subtopic: LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to advise the house that this morning I had discussions with representatives of the longshoremen concerning the dispute involving dock operations in Montreal, Three Rivers and Quebec
city. These representatives were gravely concerned with respect to misleading and erroneous reports to the effect that the government was holding the club of compulsory arbitration over the heads of the parties to the dispute, and that the government had decided to impose compulsory arbitration to effect a settlement of the dispute.
Here and now, Mr. Speaker, and in the strongest possible terms I wish to state that the government has made no threats of compulsory arbitration directly or indirectly and, further, that the government has made no decision with respect to imposing compulsory arbitration by legislation. We have appointed a mediator who is engaged in a sustained and intensive effort to settle the dispute on a voluntary basis, and I am in full agreement with the representatives of the longshoremen that innocent or malicious speculation regarding the imposition of arbitration can have nothing but an inhibiting effect on the efforts of Judge Lippe. I have received tributes to the skill and patience of Judge Lippe in this difficult situation.
Finally, I would refer members of the house to my statement last Friday. Both parties in this dispute have complied fully with our labour law and are free now to engage in other processes available to them under that law. We have gone beyond our usual efforts to assist the parties because of the national importance of a resumption of the dock operations. The government expects the parties, by voluntary methods and with the able assistance of the mediator, to work out their economic affairs in good faith, and I hope this statement will assist them to that end. Meanwhile Judge Lippe is continuing his efforts and will discuss with the parties this afternoon, as he did to the early hours of this morning, proposals for the settlement of the dispute.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    TRANSFER OF OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    TRANSFER OF OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement concerning Trans-Canada Air Lines overhaul and maintenance facilities at Winnipeg, the Dixon-Speas study and matters arising out of it.
On the basis of full and confidential information involving T.C.A.'s forward planning

Trans-Canada Air Lines of its operations for the next 10 years, the consultants think that the most economic course for T.C.A. would be to close the Winnipeg facilities.
Both T.C.A. and the government recognize that, while this is indeed an important consideration, there are other factors which have to be considered too. T.C.A., therefore, stands by its previous decision to maintain the Winnipeg facilities until 1966.
Now that the Dixon-Speas report has provided full information on one aspect of the problem, the government will consider this in relation to other aspects, the general shape of national aviation policy and policies for regional economic development and manpower adjustment. The decision as to whether the Winnipeg facilities should be adapted for use beyond 1966 will be based on all these considerations, as the Prime Minister has promised it would be. The government appreciates the importance to the people affected, of an early decision. Therefore, complex though the problem is, it expects to come to a conclusion by the end of the year.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    TRANSFER OF OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext:
We have been waiting with a great deal of interest and some impatience for a report by the minister. We had hoped that he would have given the house and the country a decision by the government right now. He has not given us any additional information. We have been aware that the recent technical report dealt with the economic factors. We have been aware also that the government, through the Prime Minister and others, has made commitments to the people of Winnipeg and the employees of T.C.A. that other factors would be considered.
There is nothing new, therefore, in what the minister has now stated except that other matters are going to be decided upon before the decision is reached. He mentioned, I believe, a policy with regard to regional industrial development and aviation policy; and his colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs was reported somewhat earlier to the effect that there was a third policy, job displacement and regional manpower adjustment. These three policies have to be formulated and implemented, according to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, before a decision is reached concerning T.C.A. overhaul and maintenance base.
This means a great deal of unnecessary delay, in our opinion, and is very frustrating indeed to the employees of T.C.A. in Winnipeg and to the general economy of that great city.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES WINNIPEG    TRANSFER OF OVERHAUL AND MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext:
I am
certain that the statement made by the minister today will be a great disappointment to

everybody in the greater Winnipeg area. This is a subject which has received unanimous support from all sectors of the province, labour, management, business and provincial and municipal governments. The Prime Minister, the minister and other members of the government met a large delegation here last May, and the Prime Minister made it clear that the economic effect of this move on T.C.A. would not be the only consideration which would be looked at by the government. In other words, something besides the mere saving of money by T.C.A. would be considered.
We are all disappointed that the report to which the minister referred has been kept secret and has not been made available to the interested parties. It is our understanding that the only thing the report says is that T.C.A. would save money. There is nothing in the report which changes the original contention of the parties that the move would be a real blow to the province of Manitoba and to the greater Winnipeg area, and a tremendous hardship on the people who work for T.C.A. in Winnipeg who would be forced to move to Montreal.
There is nothing in the minister's statement which would at all allay these fears, and I certainly join with the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre in expressing disappointment that the people of Winnipeg will again have to wait, this time until the end of 1963. On the basis of past experience with T.C.A. in this problem, at the end of 1963 we will probably hear that it will take until the end of 1964.
What we are worried about, aside from this delay, is that while this is going on T.C.A. will continue the process of the last 10 years of chipping away the whole position of T.C.A. in Winnipeg. Despite all the assurances of T.C.A. and ministers of transport, there has been a continuous drop in T.C.A. jobs at Winnipeg, and I hope the minister would at least make it clear to T.C.A. that there should be no reduction of jobs in Winnipeg, and no transfers from Winnipeg to Montreal, until the government has enunciated its policy much more clearly than the minister did today.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND BULGARIA

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND BULGARIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce that on behalf of the government of Canada I have just signed a three year trade agreement between Canada and the People's Republic of Bulgaria. In connection with the negotiation of the agreement it has been my pleasure to welcome to

Ottawa Mr. I. Boudinov, Bulgarian minister of foreign trade, who is in the gallery today witnessing our proceedings.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND BULGARIA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND BULGARIA
speechtext:
Mr. Boudinov signed the agreement on behalf of the government of his country. The agreement provides for an exchange of most favoured nation treatment between our two countries, and a commitment by the People's Republic of Bulgaria to purchase a minimum of 100,000 metric tons of wheat in each of the three years of the agreement. However, Bulgaria will purchase an additional 150,000 metric tons of Canadian wheat, subject to the Canadian supply position, during the current crop year, and the way is open for both parties to negotiate for even greater quantities in the future. At buyer's option, all or part of the above mentioned quantities of wheat may be taken in flour equivalent.
The agreement provides for consultation between representatives of the two governments respecting implementation of the agreement, should this be required. In addition, it has been agreed that trade offices may be opened both in Canada and Bulgaria for the purposes of market exploration and trade promotion. The conclusion of successful negotiations followed preliminary talks which have taken place between representatives of the two countries over several months.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND BULGARIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house and the country will be very well pleased to hear that the minister is taking advantage of the tremendous demand for products of this country in countries behind the iron curtain. There was no secret about the fact that over the last two or three years this demand was rising and these countries were in the market for long term agreements for our products, and that we in return would have to make them some concessions in order to get into our markets here. I only hope the most favoured nation treatment that has been granted to Bulgaria today will result in considerable trade between our two countries, and I hope the government keeps up this program of dealing with countries behind the iron curtain.
I would like to mention this specifically. On August 3 last I gave a list of countries which I think would be interested in receiving the same type of treatment. If the minister would go to Hungary, for example, I think he could probably make an agreement for 300,000 tons a year. I think this could be done by giving them most favoured nation treatment.
I would like to congratulate the government for its wisdom in following the sound policies already well established.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to welcome the announcement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce respecting both the specified quantities of wheat that have been sold to Bulgaria and also the fact that most favoured nation trade arrangements have been set up with that republic. I therefore hope there will be a very high degree of co-operation among the Department of Transport, the labour unions and others involved in order that we are able to meet the delivery commitments. maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND BULGARIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all Canadians will welcome the announcement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the effect that a trade agreement has been entered into with the government of Bulgaria, that this will involve sales of Canadian wheat over the next three years, and that in return we will be extending to Bulgaria the most favoured nation provisions.
I think the government is wise in recognizing two basic principles; first, that we ought to be prepared to sell food and other non-strategic materials to any country which is willing to pay for them either in cash or on a credit basis. I think the second principle which is recognized, and I hope they will continue to recognize it, is that if we are to sell export commodities like wheat we must be prepared to accept some of the goods of other countries in exchange. We cannot have one way trade; trade is a two way proposition. Certainly the government is wise in exploring the whole field of what goods from these other countries we can accept so as to enable them to earn the necessary Canadian dollars with which to pay for the wheat.
I would like to say one other word; that some of the ministers who have been advising western farmers that they had better get out of wheat will probably now have to reverse this advice. I am convinced that the wheat acreage on the prairies could be greatly expanded and that there will be no difficulty in increasing the production of wheat if that is necessary to meet these further orders.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish today

National Power Policy to announce on behalf of the government a national power policy. I do not think I have to emphasize the vital role the power industry is playing and must continue to play in the development of our nation. The story of the electric power industry of today is one of constant evolution as it strives successfully to reduce costs. Canada must provide the climate in which we can take advantage of these technical breakthroughs.
Our policy places particular emphasis on (a) the desirability of Canada taking fullest advantage of the evolutionary changes that have taken place in the nature of the power industry, including technological improvements in generating and transmission facilities, and the reduced costs of power associated with these; (b) the provision of abundant supplies of electrical energy to consumers throughout Canada at the lowest possible cost to encourage and accelerate economic development and growth; (c) the need for Canada to have a flexible export policy which, inter alia, would permit the export of large blocks of power to the United States for a relatively long period of years to assist in the immediate development of certain large scale Canadian power projects, particularly undeveloped hydro resources which might not be viable in the near future unless provision were made for the marketing in the United States of a significant portion of their output; and (d) the strengthening of our balance of payments position through the export of power surplus to our own needs.
The policy now being announced reflects important changes which have taken place in the circumstances affecting export of power. The government is fully aware of the body of public opinion that has been opposed to export of power, in the first instance because of events which occurred over 50 years ago.
The National Energy Board Act now provides that all exports of power must be licensed by the national energy board with the approval of the governor in council. Licences may not be issued for a term in excess of 25 years. The national energy board is required to certify that the power to be exported does not exceed the surplus remaining after due allowance has been made for the reasonably foreseeable requirements for use in Canada, and this has been interpreted to mean surplus to Canadian requirements which can be supplied economically from the generating facilities producing the power for export. Further, the board must satisfy itself that the export price of the power is just and reasonable in relation to the public interest.
From 1907 until the coming into force in 1959 of the National Energy Board Act, the

export of power was subject to licence under the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act. By regulation under that act the term of a licence was limited to one year. This was intended to prevent permanent alienation of Canadian power capacity which, though surplus when installed would be required in Canada as time went on. It was realized that if an industry or a community in the United States became dependant on a Canadian power supply it would be difficult, if not impossible, to withdraw that supply.
Such difficulties as have occurred in respect of the recapture of power exports arose in part because over 50 years ago long term contracts-up to 85 years-were made by Canadian power producers with specific industries in the United States. The contracts contained no provisions for the repatriation of the power. The Canadian supplier, in effect, had taken on within the United States the responsibility of a public utility to maintain continuity of supply for its customers. As a result, the protection of the one year limitation on licences was illusory.
The nature of the power industry today is very different from what it was in 1907 and in most of the intervening years. It is now unusual for the capacity of a large, modern electric plant to be dedicated to a single industry, or for a large utility to be dependant on one source of power supply. We are entering the era of large private and public electrical utilities, interlinked with high voltage lines and operated pursuant to interconnection agreements designed to take advantage of the new technological improvements and the economies of scale.
A public utility, whether in Canada or the United States, now takes it as a matter of course that it must contract for or instal capacity to replace a portion of its total power supply when the contract covering that portion runs out. The old aphorism that an export sale, once established, cannot be terminated without hardship in the export market and danger of international friction is no longer valid if the export contract is made with a public utility in the United States under reasonable terms and conditions.
When the National Energy Board Act came into effect in 1959, power export licences which had been issued under the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act were continued in effect for some time, so that the board might apply to each case with minor exceptions the procedure of application, public hearing, detailed analysis and recommendation to the governor in council.
In 1959 actual total exports, as distinguished from licensed authorizations, were 4,582 mil-

lion kilowatt hours. In 1962 export had declined to 89 per cent of the 1959 total. In 1962 Canada produced 117 billion kilowatt hours, including 11.4 per cent from thermoelectric plants. Of the total production, only 0.47 per cent was exported as firm energy and 2.8 per cent as interruptible energy. Of the latter, 86 per cent was interchanged with United States utilities, having been returned to Canada at the same time over other circuits, or over the same circuits at other times.
In the light of the circumstances I have outlined the government has decided to develop and carry forward effective policies embracing two essential concepts; first, encouraging development of large low cost power sources and the distribution of the benefits thereof as widely as possible through interconnection between power systems within Canada; second, encouraging power exports and interconnections between Canadian and United States power systems where such induce early development of Canadian power resources.
More specifically, our policy is as follows. The government, having due regard to the rights of the provinces with respect to the development and distribution of power, and keeping in mind its own responsibilities in this field, desires to encourage interconnection agreements and maximum utilization of intertie facilities between electrical systems, both publicly and privately owned. The government, in co-operation with the provinces, has already undertaken studies to investigate the possibility of interconnecting power systems across the country. It realizes that the complete interconnection may not be economically feasible for some years to come. Nevertheless, it would appear that by establishment of interconnection facilities between utilities in adjacent regions, wherever practical, a national system might be developed by a succession of stages, each valuable in itself.
The government believes that it would be beneficial to Canada and to the United States, and not prejudicial to the national interest, to encourage interconnection agreements and interties between utilities in the respective countries in cases where the interconnection agreements suitably protect the Canadian interest. In cases in which Canadian utilities enter into appropriate interconnection agreements with United States utilities, the government will be prepared, upon recommendation of the national energy board, to give favourable consideration to the authorization of export of power to United States utilities for purposes including the following. First, to provide stand-by service in the case of emergencies, thus making possible the reduction of reserve generating capacity otherwise required by the utilities; second, to provide 28902-5-211i
National Power Policy for economy flows between plants or systems; third, to provide for sales of surplus interruptible energy; fourth, to provide for exchange of power and energy to take advantage of load, watershed or other diversities; and fifth, to provide for exports of firm power for limited periods to make possible the step by step construction of the most economical generating facilities on either side of the boundary.
The government also believes that it would be in the national interest, in suitable cases, to license the export of large blocks of firm power to United States utilities to permit the development of large scale remote hydro or other power projects which would not be viable unless supported by the export for long periods of a significant proportion of the power generated. The National Energy Board Act permits such exports for periods of up to 25 years. Provision would have to be made for the recapture of such exported power over a period of years, in stages commensurate with the need or ability of the Canadian market to absorb it, and upon notice adequate to enable the importing utility to arrange for replacements. The provisions of the National Energy Board Act would, of course, apply to any case of this nature, as to any export of power.
The government will, upon recommendation of the national energy board, continue to authorize the export of relatively small amounts of power and energy to border areas in the United States where, for geographical reasons, Canada is the economic source of supply.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the long disquisition by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was summarized in about two lines in the speech from the throne in 1962 presented by the government of which I had the honour to be the head.
The minister went back to 1907 and dealt with the statute of that time which denied the export of power, and he left the impression that this announcement today was something that represented cogitation and consideration by the present government. I would point out this fact; that three years ago we took the stand that the rules which had heretofore been in effect denying export should be removed, and that export of power surplus over and above foreseeable needs could be made to the United States. In addition, at the same time or somewhat earlier we established the national energy board in order to bring about power development in Canada which would assure our future needs and we gave that board the power to recommend the export of power subject to the

National Power Policy
agreement of the governor in council. All these things were done under the previous government.
The announcement made today adds thereto the establishment of a national grid. This was part and parcel of our policy, a policy for which we received little support from those who now sit opposite. Much is made of the fact that consideration is now being given to preserving and maintaining provincial rights in this connection. That, too, is a welcome change on the part of the government. We had negotiations under way for the establishment of a national grid. In short, this announcement was made by us several years ago-
Oh, oh.

However, in the words of a familiar quotation, while the lamp holds out to burn the wandering sinner may return, and we are glad to see that hon. gentlemen opposite have repented of their former attitude.

I rise only to say I am very pleased indeed with the announcement which has been made this afternoon in connection with power policy. For some time now there has been a dire need for changes to be made in the policy of the federal government relating to power and power distribution in Canada.
I may say I am not interested in the pot calling the kettle black or in the skunk saying "I smell something", if that is a better term. I am not interested in recriminations of that kind. I am interested in the progress that is being made, whether it began with the Conservative party or with the Liberal party; and I think if they are honest hon. members in all parties will be bound to admit that the difference between the two parties is very slight.
However, I know the province of British Columbia in particular will welcome this announcement. I can see that it is likely to have a direct effect on the plans which that government has for the development of the Peace river and of the Columbia river basin. This is of importance to the people of Canada as a whole, as was pointed out in the statement which the minister made, inasmuch as it concerns the arrangements made for the exchange of power between this country and the United States.
In conclusion I should like to renew a plea to the government that they give serious consideration to the establishment of a department of federal-provincial affairs. The circumstances surrounding this announcement provide one more illustration of the need for setting up such a department. As I say, we welcome the announcement and I am sure it

will go a long way toward making possible the development which is to take place in the province of British Columbia, a development which will create markets for the manufacturing centres of eastern Canada.

This is much too important and complex a matter to be dealt with on motions on the orders of the day, and it seems to me some early opportunity should be given for a full debate on the subject by this parliament. This is a matter of far reaching importance to the people of Canada, and I hope the government will find an opportunity to arrange for a fuller discussion at an early date.
There are two aspects of the minister's statement upon which I should like to comment. The first has to do with the establishment of a national power grid. This is a project which has interested many of us for a number of years. Some progress has been made by utilities concerned, both public and private, as well as by the provincial governments in their discussions over the past few years, but I should like to say this to the minister. In our view the public and private power utilities of Canada do not merely require assistance in conducting studies. A good many studies have already been conducted, and I think the companies are able to undertake such studies without any great measure of assistance. The real problem which the power utilities face is the heavy capital expenditure which will have to be made if a national power grid is to be established.
New techniques have now made it possible to transmit power over long distances without a heavy line loss. In Sweden they are now transmitting power some 1500 miles without serious power loss and, I learned from engineers there, that in the Soviet union they are carrying power over distances even greater than this. But these developments require heavy capital expenditure, and if the government really wishes to help develop a national power grid it will, I believe, have to be prepared to make loans available to the public and private utilities so that construction may be undertaken with the result that wherever there is cheap power available in our part of Canada, it may be made available in other parts of the country. This would avoid part of our present deficit on our balance of payments account, because at the present time we are spending large sums on the purchase of United States coal for central Canada to provide power through thermal units.
The second point I have to make concerns the export of power. I would say that if the government now proposes to agree to the export of power there are two conditions

which ought to be laid down in order to safeguard the interests of the Canadian people. First, no power should be exported if it can be used to advantage in Canada. We should not be exporting Canadian power if it can be used near the point of production or transmitted to a part of Canada which could use it economically.
I do not know whether the government made this announcement today as a prelude to some decision with reference to the Columbia river development, but I think before any final agreement is signed with the province of British Columbia the whole question of that development should be submitted to the committee of external affairs of this house in order that the entire subject may be reviewed, and witnesses like General MacNaughton called, in order that hon. members may be fully aware of the situation. I say this because we are dealing here not only with the export of power but with the release of all the water of the fifth largest river on the North American continent. It is a most important matter and I hope it will not be referred to the committee on external affairs only after an agreement is signed and the house is faced with a fait accompli.
The second thing I wish to say about the export of power is that agreements for the export of firm blocks of power-arrangements for stand-by or emergency power are another matter-should be permitted only if there is provision for the progressive withdrawal of that power in blocks over a period of years in order to meet the growing needs of Canada. Power demand is increasing at an amazingly rapid rate, and we could easily sign long term commitments for power which we ourselves would need in the course of the next ten, 20 or 30 years.
I hope that the energy board will be instructed by the minister to see that in any export permits which are granted, there is adequate provision that this power can be restored to Canada as our demand load grows.

Since the establishment of the agricultural prices stabilization board and up to March 31, 1963, what has been paid as a grant of 25 cents per hundredweight of milk to the operators of each of the following factories:

speechtext: I made a statement at the resolution stage. The bill is now before the house, as it has been for several days. It consists of only two clauses, the first giving the increase and the second dealing with the method of financing, and I suggest that in order to leave sufficient time to allow hon. members opposite to say whatever they wish to say about the bill there is no necessity for me to make a further statement on this occasion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
I agree with the minister's comment that this is a brief bill containing only two clauses, the first indicating the increase in the amount as of October 1 and the second providing the means by which this increase is to be financed.

I feel I cannot let the occasion pass without repeating a statement I made at an earlier stage to the effect that we, on this side of the house, had advocated this particular move -the bringing in of this bill separately-as far back as July 18. I repeat, also, that if this had been done at that time, and if our advice had been followed, the recipients of old age security benefits would have received this $10 increase considerably earlier. We are pleased to see that the government has now adopted our proposal and dissociated this part of the pension plan from the over-all Pearson plan, something which should have been done in the first place.
This is something which was promised by the government during the election campaign.
I am convinced it is being put into effect, now, only because of prompting from this side of the house. In my opinion this whole question has been mishandled in much the same way as was the budget. First of all, the government came out with a grand scheme in a hurry, and then it backtracked under pressure. I accuse the minister of doing the same thing now.
Clause 2 of the bill deals with the financing of this proposal-the levying of 4 per cent of a taxpayer's taxable income for the year to a maximum of $120. In speaking on the resolution stage, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) said the total deficit in the fund as at March 31, 1964 would be $106 million. He went on to point out that in the year 1964-65 there would probably be receipts from the new tax amounting to some $93 million and that about $116 million would be paid out. However, some increase in revenue from the sales tax on building materials and supplies would probably wipe out any deficit in that year. Thus, it seems to me that for a year and a half hence, at least, taking the figures of the parliamentary secretary as accurate, there will be a deficit in this fund of $106 million. The hon. gentleman gave estimates of certain increases in revenue and I ask him whether he had taken into consideration the natural increase to be expected in the numbers of those over 70 who would be receiving old age security payments a year and a half or two years from now. My main criticism is simply this. The government said they were going to increase old age security payments without any increase in taxes. This is not so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext: Broken promises.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
They are increasing taxes $93 million, according to the parliamentary secretary's own estimate, in the year 196465 and roughly $100 million a year thereafter. They no sooner got into power than they clamped a sales tax on building materials

and supplies and now we have a 1 per cent increase in personal income tax up to a maximum of $120. This may not be the time to do it, but with all these increases in taxes I certainly must predict an over-all record budgetary deficit. However, that can be discussed at some time in the future.
We are anxious to get this legislation through, and we have been ever since it came before the house. We are more than happy to support the bill. I suggest very forcefully that if it had not been for the actions of the Leader of the Opposition on July 18 the older citizens of Canada would not be receiving this increase even as of the late date of October 1, 1963.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just spoken seems to wish to leave the impression with the House of Commons and the people of Canada that certain statements made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) are the reason that the $10 increase is now being proposed-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext: Made in this house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
-although it was originally linked with the Canada pension plan introduced earlier this year. I should like to suggest that perhaps some of the problems encountered by the government in their negotiations with the provincial governments may have had a great bearing on bringing in this increase separately. I think that some of the very real problems they did have in discussing the over-all pension plan with the provinces should have been anticipated and that negotiations should have been carried on long before the resolution was even introduced in the house.
We know, of course, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh), along with her colleagues, got caught in their 60 days of decision propaganda, if you want to call it that. Because of the 60 days of decision, as they prefer to call them, I think there was undue haste in bringing in the over-all Canada pension plan. I believe they have now come to realize that the pension plan is of such magnitude it is absolutely necessary that some agreement be reached with the provinces rather than bringing it in in an ill-conceived way, and this realization should give them some kind of guidance in trying to convince the electorate these things can be done quickly.
We support the bringing in of the $10 increase separately, and while it may be another violation of Liberal election propaganda I personally think it is desirable that the amount of additional taxes necessary to pay for it should be fastened right to the
Old Age Security
bill. I say that because I think there is growing concern in Canada that political parties have on a number of occasions tried to outbid each other in offering benefits without bothering to tell the people how much it is going to cost them. Now that we have legislation before us offering increased benefits, with the bill for these benefits attached to it, perhaps this will sober the response of the electorate to those political parties who offer benefits, and then worry about paying for them with deficits such as we have seen in the last four or five years.
I do not wish to take a great deal of time. I believe that all parties in the house can support the bill and I do not think there is going to be any division, because members voting for it will also have to assume the responsibility of making provision for the collecting of the money to pay for these benefits.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak briefly on second reading of the bill, not to repeat the arguments that were advanced at the resolution stage but to develop a point of principle which was touched on but not elaborated upon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I do not refer to the principle embodied in clause 1 of the bill. This clause, as members realize, provides for an increase in the pension to $75 a month. With that proposal we and all other members of the house, I understand, are heartily in accord. We have expressed as clearly as we can our approval of this move. It is our view that this matter should be separated from the complexities of the Canada pension plan and dealt with promptly. Indeed, we think it should have been dealt with earlier than it has been.
However, Mr. Speaker, it is the principle involved in clause 2 of the bill that I wish to discuss. I wish to say that in our view the principle in clause 2 is wrong and ought to be changed. That clause deals with the question of how the additional moneys required for the increased pension should be raised.
It is our opinion that the method proposed in clause 2 of the bill is wrong in principle, regressive, and fails to take advantage of the possibility of giving a dynamic stimulus to the economy which is inherent in the proposed pension increase. The proposal in clause 2, as members will realize in reading the bill, is to increase the rate of tax on all taxable income to 4 per cent instead of the present rate of 3 per cent, and to raise the ceiling on the tax to $120 in place of the $90 under the present act.
We say that, assuming the decision of the government not to add to the prospective

Old Age Security
deficit, the proper way to raise the funds necessary to finance the increase, assuming as the government does the necessity of doing so, would be to remove the ceiling and leave the tax at the same rate of 3 per cent. By removing the ceiling, now $90, and $120 in the proposal, roughly enough money would be raised-I have inquired into this-to pay the whole of the increase without any other addition to taxes.
If our plan were adopted the effect would be that the increase would be paid by taxpayers whose taxable income exceeds $3,000 a year or whose actual income, to take an average case, is in the neighbourhood of $5,000 a year. Our proposal would relieve income taxpayers below that figure of any additional burden. We believe this solution would be economically wise and socially just.
When this measure was first introduced in the house in 1951 by a previous administration the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the same hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who sits in the house today, made these remarks. I am not going to quote extensively from what he said, but as found on page 397 of Hansard, second session, 1951, he said:
I refer in particular to his statement-
The statement by the minister of finance. -that this 2 per cent personal income tax is to have a ceiling of $60 a year. That means that anyone who has taxable income-and I emphasize the words "taxable income": that is, income over and above his personal and family exemptions-of more than $3,000 a year, will pay no old age security tax on the portion of his income that is above that $3,000. I regard that situation as grossly unfair. It means that the bulk of the burden of financing the old age security plan will be met through the sales tax on everybody, including those who cannot afford to pay it, and through the income tax on the middle income group, those in the brackets where they have taxable income of between $2,000 and $3,000 a year.
Later on page 398 of Hansard, the hon. member is reported as saying:
The Minister of Finance comes along today and tells us that the principle of excluding upper income has been included in this plan, with the result, as I say, that people who have over $3,000 of taxable income will not pay any old age security tax on that portion of their income above $3,000 a year. I think that is socially and economically wrong. I think it is completely indefensible, and for my part it will have to be fought as hard as we can fight it when we get to that part of the bill.
I venture to repeat what the hon. member then said made good sense. If it made good sense then, it makes even better sense today, and for this reason. Placing the burden of this additional and necessary tax on the lower and middle income groups and relieving the upper income groups by maintaining the $120 ceiling is a regressive and uneconomic measure. The increase in old age pensions is not only a belated measure of justice to older people who are in need, it is also needed to

give a fillip to the economy. This $10 will be spent largely by old age pensioners on consumer goods in small retail stores. This will be a dynamic impetus to a stagnating economy. Typical of this government, what they give with one hand they take away with the other. The imposition of the additional 1 per cent tax and the maintenance of the ceiling means that, in effect, the tax burden will be borne entirely by the people in the lower and middle income brackets. The taxpayers in the higher income brackets will go free. It is the people in the lower and middle income brackets, Mr. Speaker, who, it can be assumed, would spend their income in purchasing consumer goods. The effect of this tax, as proposed by the government, will be to reduce the purchasing power of this lower and middle income group, thereby undoing the good that is done, economically speaking, by the increasing of the old age pension.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this difference between the government and the members of this party represents a fundamental cleavage of opinion on principle. Apparently the Liberal party does not see the power of taxation as we do, as an instrument of social justice for the redistribution of income. We believe that social advances, such as increased and more adequate old age pensions and a national health plan are not only important in themselves, they are also a means for allowing the well-to-do to contribute their proportionate share to the provision of essential services for those who cannot afford to pay for them themselves. In other words, measures of social security should be financed in accordance with ability to pay. It should not be a principle, as we have it embodied in this particular act, that the well-to-do should be relieved of the burden and those in the lower brackets should be asked to assume that burden. In our opinion this is contrary to sound, fundamental principles.
To put the matter as simply as I can, the proposal which we make would put the burden of supplying the $115 million which is required upon those whose taxable income exceeds $3,000 a year and whose actual income, in most cases, would be in excess of $5,000 a year. The government proposal, on the other hand, is that the burden shall be borne by the taxpayers below the taxable income level of $3,000 or below the average income of $5,000. I have taken the trouble to ascertain that the proposal which I make, namely of removing the ceiling altogether and keeping the tax at the same rate would, financially speaking, produce roughly the same result.
I should like to illustrate the point I am making by referring to hon. members of this

house. Under the government's proposal, their contribution to this increase in the old age pension, or their total payment towards old age pensions, would be $120 because they would be able to take advantage of the ceiling proposed. The main purpose of this bill is to establish in Canada a national sweepstakes board to manage, run and control sweepstakes in Canada. I added the words "to manage and control sweepstakes in Canada'' because in many facets of our life in Canada today we have, although they might not be called sweepstakes, what are certainly huge lotteries, gambling by tickets, and so on. One has only to look around to realize that this is a fact. In fact, Mr. Speaker, you can now play bingo when sitting at home watching the television. This is an interesting form of gambling, to some extent.
Throughout Canada I think there is a wide demand that the federal government establish once and for all a sweepstakes board and that the function of this board be to set up a national sweepstake in Canada. One could go back and read all the press clippings of responsible groups which are in favour of such a board being established. I have here a newspaper clipping which states that the federation of Canadian mayors and municipalities passed a resolution in favour of a national lottery. From time to time Gallup polls on this question have been taken. A recent one showed that 82 per cent of Canadians were in favour of a national sweepstake. A poll taken by a well-known paper in the province of Quebec, La Presse, showed that of 98,000 people polled only 149 were against the establishment of a sweepstake. Two years ago, I think it was, a group of women took it upon themselves to campaign across Canada in order to determine whether or not a national sweepstake had universal appeal. They covered an area of something like 12,000 miles, talked to a huge number of people, received some 300,000 signatures, and at no time met anyone who was strongly opposed to the establishment of a national sweepstake. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce has passed resolutions endorsing the principle outlined in this bill. Nearly all the Canadian labour unions have also endorsed the establishment of a national sweepstake.

Apparently the proponent of the bill also has the thought in mind that lottery revenues will be such as to lessen the tax burden to a substantial degree in some way. If we are going to consider such bills, then I suggest we should consider the facts as they are and not as we would like them to be. The hon. member for Acadia referred to statistics from New Zealand which would indicate that, having regard to the large amounts of money put into lotteries, the amount available for beneficial work on the part of the state, be it hospitals or otherwise, is very little. I think this has been the experience with lotteries. It may appear as though there is a great deal of money going into them, and a great deal does; but the returns to the state are not as great as we would expect from the turnover of money involved. Possibly this is because of administrative expenses or the fact that if people are handling gambling money in an enterprise of this kind they are not as careful with it as they are in handling general tax revenues, and therefore the expenses are greater.
The hon. member for Acadia indicated he was anxious to have some of the smaller and poorer provinces share in the benefits that would flow from this bill. I do not think

he would want his province to become the Nevada of Canada. I do not think we want a Las Vegas here. These things are a matter oi degree, and judging by the New Zealand experience in particular I do not believe that the returns from this kind of investment warrant a new form of taxation at the present time.
I quite agree with my hon. friend that on this topic, like so many other controversial topics, the majority of the people of Canada should have the right to speak. It may be that this is the type of matter that could be put before the public by way of plebiscite. It may be sufficiently important to do so. I feel there is one aspect we should consider in connection with this matter. Of late years, this type of suggestion has been very popular. I believe we should give some thought as to why, all of a sudden, this type of painless taxation, as it is supposed to be, has come to the forefront and has won the approval of so many members and of so many segments of the public. It may be that this is a symptom of the age. There has been a thought in the minds of people, probably more in this country than elsewhere in the past few years, that in some magic way, by some waving of a magic wand, revenues can be raised to do all those things we wish to do for our people without paying, without effort and without digging in as we used to do.
Evidently the attitude is that this is the easiest method. It is painless. It is fun. Everybody has a good time. We raise the revenues we need for the things we want to do. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner), who sponsored this bill, spoke of the moral fibre. Taking his argument to its logical conclusion, this would mean that the people with the toughest moral fibre would be the inhabitants of Las Vegas because they gamble more than anybody else. I do not believe this is necessarily a proper conclusion. Even if lotteries would do no harm, even if they might raise some revenue painlessly, I still have some qualms about this suggestion. I think that to propagate a national philosophy at this time that there is an easy way, that there is something for nothing, that we can have a higher standard of living in this land by some easy and painless method, that we can have more social benefits for our people without paying the price for those social benefits, is dangerous.
We have seen how well the people of Germany and Japan, those lands that were decimated by the war, have re-established themselves since the end of the war. No doubt this has been the result of the help the allies gave, to some considerable measure. However, I think we must pause for a moment and reflect upon the way Germany and Japan in

particular have come back. This has resulted, to a very large degree, from the fact that the people were willing to work, to make sacrifices, I do not believe they expected great social benefits. The unions held the line in wages, and I think capital held the line in dividends. These people pulled together as a nation and, because of the decimation of the war, they were willing to do so. They had something for which they were willing to work, to rebuild their countries, and they have done so to a large degree. People who have been to Europe and Japan during the past few years tell us that there is no unemployment, that there is an increasing standard of living. There is this national philosophy, apparently, that the people of the country must work hard and pull together if they are to achieve the things they wish.
The politicians here have certainly been guilty of propagating the idea of getting something for nothing. Vote for A or vote for B or vote for party one or party two, and you can have all these things that you would like to have without any national effort. I feel this is a very dangerous thing in our Canadian political thinking. This is a great land of boundless opportunity. Our people can have all the things they would like to have, but they cannot have them through the use of any magic formula or in any easy way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, here is another matter which carries a full range of arguments. We shall add to it, if possible.
Arguments on grounds of moral, ethics and religion are put forward against lotteries. However, hardly a Sunday goes by without a Canadian minister or priest asking his flock to make a donation to such and such organization by buying a raffle ticket. So, I fail to see how a national or provincial lottery could be such a sin when it is not in the case of the charities recommended by those priests and ministers.
If we take a look at the newspapers for a knowledge of the public opinion, we see-as has already been said here-that the newspaper La Presse, a few years ago, made a survey on that matter which revealed that out of 100,000 people only 149 were against the setting up of a lottery. The Toronto Telegram, in a survey on the same subject which it carried out also a few years ago, received 8,990 answers in favour of lotteries against 814 opposed to them; and about 700 people admitted having bought in the past lottery tickets from various organizations.

On the other hand, the most convincing argument for the adoption of such legislation is to keep Canadian money in Canada. As far as I know, nobody has ever objected to the stock exchange transactions. Nobody has ever objected to the hazards of life. In a certain sense, aren't both of them a gamble? And yet who would consider prohibiting them?
The lack of money therefore remains a temptation for our rulers to encourage lotteries. If you look at a number of countries in the world, you notice that during the past few years, many countries have adopted that solution.
Australia has organized five annual lotteries and a newspaperman stated that lotteries are a means of survival in that country thanks to the profits brought in to the public, the government, the hospitals and charitable institutions.
As was said earlier, New Zealand established in 1961 a lottery called "The Golden Kiwi". It has been so successful that they even wondered for a time how to distribute the profits.
France keeps 40 per cent of the proceeds of its lottery, which does not prevent that country from awarding a $100,000 prize to the winner. West Germany has its lottery since 1955. Austria established a lottery in 1813. Italy has four big lotteries every year which are held by means of horse races, car races or even popular songs.
Switzerland, Portugal, Spain and most Latin American countries hold private or public lotteries, not to mention countries behind the iron curtain, such as East Germany, Poland and Soviet Russia, which also have their own lotteries.
Israel, where any form of gambling is prohibited, including horse racing, has nevertheless established a state lottery which yields $8 million a year. The money is used to build schools and hospitals. And yet, this is a country where all types of gambling are prohibited.
It is common knowledge that horse racing is organized in Canada.
Whether you are listening to the radio, looking at television or reading a newspaper, everywhere you are offered a premium of some kind or another with the purchase of a product. If that is not a lottery, I feel the principle is the same.
Moreover, the state of New Hampshire legalized lotteries recently. That will be the first legal lottery in the history of the United States since 1894. It will be held twice a year in connection with a race and tickets will be $3 each. Prizes will total $200,000 and the state will build schools with the $4 million it expects to get every year from its lotteries. In my opinion, those surveys prove beyond 28902-5-2124
Sweepstakes
doubt that the great majority of Canadians are now in favour of lotteries and I hope that the Criminal Code will soon be amended to make them legal.
At any rate, the province of Quebec has been waiting to hold a lottery for a long time. I understand that under our system of government the views of each and every province have to be respected. That is why I feel that the law should be amended so that each province may set up its own lottery if-but I doubt it very much-there are still in Canada provinces which are against lotteries.
Let there be a serious survey, let the people discuss the idea and I feel that it will soon be obvious that everybody is in favour of such a move.
Mr. Speaker, the newspaper La Presse, in its February 28, 1962 issue, published an article written by Mr. Vincent Prince. The article was entitled: Mr. Fulton must say "yes". I quote:
Premier Lesage has attempted for months to have the federal government amend section 179 of the penal code. That section, as everyone knows, has always been the obstacle which prevented the province of Quebec from fulfilling its legitimate wish to institute a provincial lottery.
Twice in the past, in 1934 and in 1950, the Quebec legislature approved measures for the institution of such lotteries, so as to give assistance to our hospitals and educational establishments. Each time, our legislators' will was frustrated by Ottawa's refusal to amend its legislation on games of chance. Indeed, it was the coming into force of that same penal code, in 1893, that put an end to the only lottery which Quebec ever had and which goes back to the days of cure Labelle.
Mr. Lesage is quite right to urge the federal Minister of Justice along, and the whole population of the province supports him. In February 1961, C.K.A.C. radio station and La Presse organized a poll, the results of which were quite revealing. One hundred thousand Quebecers answered a very precisely worded questionnaire, and barely 149 people opposed the idea of a provincial lottery. That allows us to assert that the feeling is unanimous on the subject in Quebec, as the sampling was broad enough to lead to valid conclusions.
One could naturally contemplate a nation-wide sweepstake, and actually the idea has been put forward. In the past, several resolutions have been presented to that effect in the house, but in spite of the sympathetic attitude of the Senate, none of these resolutions were concurred in. It appears clearly that there is a cleavage of Canadian opinion on that point, and many years could go by before all hon. members are in complete agreement.
That the federal government is not ready to use that type of tax, surely a direct tax, does not seem to me a worthy reason to stand in the way of the provinces which have decided to enter that field. Indeed, Mr. Lesage does not request an exclusive privilege for his province. So much the worse if the other areas of this country do not want of it.
There are still people-and I respect their opinion -who maintain that the state should not favour unrestrained gambling. And yet I think that those people are deceiving themselves. They are deceiving themselves because, in any event, few citizens do not have the opportunity to gamble. The argument would be acceptable if gambling were

Sweepstakes
an evil in itself, but such is not the case. And I am of the opinion that people will not gamble more if a lottery is set up. The difference is that the state will benefit thereby.
How many million dollars are drained from the province of Quebec at the present time by the Irish sweepstake only? Would it not be a boon if that money served our own institutions?
And what about underhand betting? What about hockey lotteries? On March 29 last, the Canadian Press informed us that $500,000 of "hockey tickets'' were sold every week in Canada. Only yesterday, the police seized 3,760,000 of those tickets on Perrot island. And it was the third confiscation of the sort in one month.
No, a provincial lottery would only channel towards Quebec state revenue which, at the present time, is going to foreign institutions or private individuals here.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of the house something that happened in Australia, I think. A young bookkeeper working in a bank managed to embezzle about $74,000 -without getting caught. One day he won first prize and decided there and then to reimburse the bank, principal and interest. That goes to show that sometimes a lottery will indeed help some people.
But, in my opinion, one very serious reason warrants holding lotteries. The article I just read mentioned the outflow of Canadian money, what are called invisible monetary deficits, which are a serious factor in our unfavourable exchange situation with foreign countries.
In that regard, I wish to read to the house an article written by Mr. Amedee Gaudreault, parliamentary correspondent for the newspaper he Soleil. Here is what he said:
Why not have a lottery?
National or provincial?
Many people think that, in Canada, a lottery should have a national character to ensure a fairer distribution of the yield among the provinces.
But if Ottawa does not want to enter that held, it should not stop one or several provinces from doing so, if they want to.
Some of us, like the hon. member for Manitoba (Mr. Regnier), suggested a national referendum. Others would like the provinces to be consulted first and say whether they are for or against the idea of a national lottery.
If the provinces were against a national lottery, they could not, later on, oppose a provincial project of that kind, first of all because they objected to a national scheme, and also to leave others free to do as they like at home.
Ottawa might amend the Criminal Code later for its own benefit or that of interested provinces, and nobody would be obliged in that case to buy lottery tickets against his will.
The recent experience in New Zealand revealed an unexpected phenomenon: a great number of tickets were sold in Australia and other countries.
If a lottery with substantial prizes were created in Canada, it is also probable, according to many observers, that such a lottery would get an important part of its revenues from the United States. It was pointed out to us that with the long Canadian-American common border, the good friendly relations between our two countries and our considerable trade deficit, it is probable that

the United States would not oppose some restoration of the balance of "invisibles" where our deficit is equally quite high, particularly in the tourist trade.
Consequently, and this is the opinion I would like to leave with this house, I am in favour of the Criminal Code being amended to allow for a lottery.

A direct result of my remarks the other day has been a letter from London, Ontario, where 50 men have now been charged in connection with the sale of sweepstakes tickets in Ontario because it is against the Criminal Code. This letter from a resident of London, who advised me

that he is one of the 50 men who have been summonsed, points out under the date of October 5:
Very shortly the horse racing season will commence at the London fair grounds. It will then be possible to enter the race track, approach a wicket, set down $2, receive a ticket and if a winner, collect in cash. This will all be under the close scrutiny of the minions of the law. Several weeks ago we staged our local London fair and here we had the opportunity of playing the roulette wheels and receiving our winnings in cash. Also under the eyes of the local police. I could go on and on adding to this list of so-called legal but out and out gambling. We live under a set of codes which are most unjust when on one hand they allow the above while on the other hand our guardians of justice will be hauling into our London court about 50 Canadian citizens who will probably have meted out to them severe judgment because of the sale of some sweepstake tickets. Australia, New Zealand, Jamaica, England, Ireland, etc. all make sweepstakes available to their citizens with no adverse effect.
This gentleman then says:
To yourself, to Guy Rouleau, to Louis Joseph Pigeon and to Barry Mather I wish you all success in your splendid efforts to amend the codes. Please tell the Prime Minister that many thousands of Canadian citizens in this area are seething at the injustice which is now prevalent under our present Criminal Code and do ask that he and his legislators take immediate action to rectify this inequality in our laws.
I can assure the writer that I will personally place this letter in the hands of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) as expressive of much of the thought that is in Canada today. Reference has been made by previous speakers to the success of the New Zealand lottery. I will not burden the house by referring to quotations they have made, but there is an interesting paragraph at the tail end of the Canadian Press dispatch on this matter. This was in the Globe and Mail of July 16, this year, and I would read it to the house:
Churches and other anti-gambling interests continue to criticize the principle.
Note the next sentence:
But public opinion is so overwhelmingly and obviously in favour of the lottery that its opponents have realized that their views cannot prevail.
I maintain that the same condition exists here in the Dominion of Canada as in New Zealand. We have before the House of Commons at the present time five private bills on this one subject introduced by private members. These five private bills have been introduced by five representatives from three different provinces in the dominion, which shows how widespread is the feeling on legalizing lotteries and sweepstakes in this country. subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the unusual harmony and agreement prevailing among all hon. members of this house in connection with the proposed $10 increase in the universal old age pension is most refreshing and is actually a striking tribute to the work done in 1950 by the joint committee of both houses of parliament on old age security, on which committee all members of this house were represented. As a result of the report of that committee the government then in office established a basic and universal pay as you go pension without a means test in the amount of $40 a month. This legislation was adopted unanimously and with universal acclaim. In

Old Age Security
its 1950 report the joint parliamentary committee emphasized that the program it recommended could be financed and administered satisfactorily only by the federal government. They said:
Only the federal authority can establish a sufficiently broad base of contributions to make such a program possible, and only the federal authority can ensure that an individual will receive the benefit to which he has contributed, regardless of whether he moves from one province to another.
All hon. members will recall that this vital report was signed by the chairmen of the committee, Senator J. H, King and the Hon. Jean Lesage, now premier of Quebec.
The $40 old age pension without a means test commenced on January 1, 1952. From 1952 to 1956, with balanced budgets and no inflation, the purchasing power of the pension expressed in constant 1952 dollars was well maintained. In 1957, as a result of two successive increases, the pension was raised to $55, but with the inflation which commenced in that year the purchasing power of that $55 pension was actually only $52.56 in constant 1952 dollars. This was a 31 per cent increase over the initial $40 pension. In the same period average weekly wages and salaries expressed in constant 1952 dollars had increased by only 21 per cent, much more slowly than the increase in pension benefits.
Hon. members of the house will recall a continuing series of massive budget deficits experienced between 1957 and 1962 totalling some $3 billion. As a result Canada experienced a continuing and accelerating inflation, and by 1962 the $55 pension had been reduced to $49 expressed in terms of constant 1952 dollars. In 1962 the pension was increased to $65, this being the equivalent of $57.94 in constant 1952 dollars. This represented a real increase of 45 per cent over the 1952 pension rate. During the same period average weekly wages and salaries had increased by 33 per cent expressed in constant dollars. When this current $10 increase in the pension is made the pension increase in constant dollars over 1952 will be 64 per cent. The increase in average wages and salaries over the same periods will be about half that, namely 37 per cent. As between 1962 and 1963 the increase in old age pensions will amount to 13 per cent, as compared with an increase in average weekly wages and salaries during the same one-year period of 3 per cent. I have documented this record, Mr. Speaker, because the concern shown by the Canadian public generally in increasing the old age pension by 64 per cent in a period in which their own wages and salaries have increased by only 37 per cent must surely be a record without parallel among other countries and one of which all Canadian taxpayers can be justly proud.

I believe that those who are now retired or on the verge of retirement would be the first to recognize this and would also be the first to insist that while appropriate respect should be paid and provision made for them, it is of prime importance to expand opportunities for those of all ages who have suffered from the massive unemployement of recent years and for the generations who will follow.
On this side of the house we believe that in this country, with the opportunities we have, we can and will do both these things.
I have emphasized that the increased pension benefits are being provided by Canadian taxpayers and not through the generosity of successive Canadian governments. The members of the government do not provide pensions and other social benefits out of their own personal funds; they merely transfer money from one group of Canadians to another, and in doing this they act as trustees and representatives of the Canadian people. Whenever the pension is increased and whenever social benefits are increased we as trustees and representatives of the Canadian people should give careful thought to the principles on which the increase is based. In considering the amount of old age pension it must be remembered that it has never been claimed that this pay-as-you-go fiat rate pension provided a proper subsistence pension for all. Speaking in the House of Commons in 1957 when the pension was raised to $55, the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith), then the minister of national health and welfare stated:
It will be sufficient in our judgment, together with the other means that most pensioners have at their disposal, to provide a decent minimum level of living for most pensioners.
The view that the hon. member for Perth so clearly expressed in 1957 is consistent with the views expressed in the 1950 report of the joint parliamentary committee. The committee at that time pointed out that the universal pay-as-you-go system is costly by its very nature and that benefit payments cannot be limited to that section of the population which can prove need, as in the case of old age assistance or to those who have previously made the required number of contributions as in the insurance approach.
The committee pointed out that considerations such as these had made it necessary for countries such as New Zealand and Sweden to set the rate of their universal benefits substantially below minimum subsistence levels. Like considerations also led the committee to the view that benefit rates under any universal system considered for Canada should not be set so high as to make the over-all cost

too burdensome. The members of the committee also pointed out that this was particularly true of a country such as Canada where living costs and wage and salary levels varied widely from one section to another. They emphasized that the rate of benefit should be set at a level which would avoid so far as possible the social inequity of a situation in which the retired beneficiary group in any area of Canada might find themselves in more favourable economic circumstances than those not yet retired who are still actually engaged in productive employment. At the same time, care should also be taken not to diminish the area of incentive for private savings or supplementary provision for old age security through employee pension schemes or individual purchases of annuities. In view of these considerations Canadians generally can take pride, I believe, in the institution of the universal old age pension without a means test and with the successive increases which have taken place and which are now proposed.
It is true that some members of the opposition parties have suggested that the increase should be made retroactive to the beginning of April and others have implied that the government has shown doubtful taste in insisting that the resolution which provided for the proposed increase should also provide the moneys required to pay that increase. Indeed, some members have gone as far as to suggest that this was a Liberal trick.

There appears to be complete unanimity among the members of this house as to the desirability of the proposed $10 increase. Some may wonder why the round figure of $10
Old Age Security
was chosen. I recall that in the early days of the Alberta oil industry, oil in the ground was customarily valued at $1 per barrel. When asked why, one operator said it was the only figure he could multiply by. Perhaps somewhat similar principles operate in leading members of parliament to favour increases by ten-dollar amounts.
But though there may be complete unanimity in this house, we must base a pension increase at this time on some logical grounds, since there is a quiet, but strong demand across the country for financial responsibility on the part of this government.
I hold in my hand a letter from a constituent who says:
I understand the government may be considering increases in corporate and personal income taxes in order to pay for the recently proposed increase in old age pensions. As one who voted for you in April, I urge you to do everything you can to prevent such an increase which would, coming at the present time, have serious and far reaching effects on the Canadian economy.
It now seems almost certain that personal and corporation taxes in the United States will be lowered in the early part of 1964. This in itself, in the absence of any parallel Canadian tax reductions, will result in a worsening of our competitive position vis-4-vis the United States. If at the same time we actually increase our taxes, Canadian industry will have a tax 'tariff' of 4 or 5 per cent to overcome in competition with United States industry, to say nothing of the inhibiting effect of tax increases on incentive.
