I have another letter from a constituent who tells me that he entered St. Michael's hospital in Toronto where he has undergone a major surgical operation for the removal of a kidney. He tells me he has been in receipt of the maximum welfare allowance of $57.10 per month and that we should recognize that in Toronto such an amount is not sufficient to provide a human being with essential food, housing and clothing. He says:
Hospitalization recently plus the costs of x-rays and a major operation is going to cost my fellow taxpayers some money. Perhaps my kidney could have been saved had I been able to secure medical treatment several months past. The miracle seems to be that I have survived, considering the fact

Old Age Security
that for months prior to the operation I was eating only the skin-and-bones food allowance of welfare recipients. If I have to continue on such a niggardly allowance it may cost my fellow taxpayers more hospitalization costs in the future. There are thousands across Canada with the same problem as myself.
I shall be glad to show this letter to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
We have been told that the $10 a month increase will mean the expenditure in a full year of $116 million. Of this amount, approximately $16 million should be recovered in income taxes, so the cost of this $10 increase will be $100 million annually and the amount will no doubt increase in future years. This huge sum of money, if received each year and properly directed and co-ordinated with expenditures of provincial governments, municipalities and the numerous charitable organizations in the field, could probably eliminate forever poverty and need among those in our country who for age or other reasons are unable to work and to provide for themselves. Yet we know that this annual expenditures of $100 million spread out in $10 monthly payments among the entire population over 70 years of age will not achieve that result.
Why then, sincere people ask, do we not mass, direct and co-ordinate all our resources in the war to eliminate forever poverty and need, instead of dissipating our available resources ineffectively in small amounts over a wide area? Why do we not use these vast sums of money to supplement income, not on the basis of the outmoded "means test" but on the basis of actual needs and without restriction to the arbitrary $10 amount?
While such arguments are persuasive, there are valid reasons for rejecting this approach and accepting, instead, a general increase in the universal pension, provided always that we can afford the increase and that the increase is provided in a manner which is consistent with financial responsibility on the part of the government. I should like to refer again to the 1950 report of the joint parliamentary committee on old age security.
In paragraphs 59 and 60 of their findings the committee said:
The committee has carefully considered the argument that such a universal system for persons 70 and over is economically wasteful in that it provides the same benefit to rich and poor alike regardless of their need. It is true, of course, that, under any system which abolished the means test for the group presently of pensionable age, benefits will be paid to some persons who do not "need" them on any test of personal need. But it must be remembered that to the extent that the universal pay as you go system is based on individual contributions, individuals in the upper income groups would, through their personal contributions, have bought and paid for their own retirement security,
[Mr. Wahn.l
as well as making a substantial contribution towards the cost of retirement security of others.
In view of these facts, the committee does not consider that it would be equitable to impose a "means test in reverse" and wholly deny retirement benefits to those individuals who have actually made the largest direct contributions to the revenues from which the universal benefits will be paid.
A certain amount of the benefits paid to persons in the upper income levels will be recovered through the normal operation of the income tax.
The committee also pointed out that to make payments to those in need while refusing payments to those who have saved during their working years to provide for their retirement has the effect of penalizing and discouraging thrift and private arrangements for old age retirement which the committee felt on the whole to be desirable to maintain. Much the same point is made in the Clark report on economic security for the aged.
These principles explain the pension arrangements for which Liberal members campaigned in the last election. We campaigned for a national contributory pension plan which would be self-supporting through contributions from those now working, and their employers.
Contrary to what has been implied by members of the opposition, we did not promise an additional $10 immediately we took office and out of general tax revenues. I hold in my hand the pamphlet which formed the basis of our election campaign entitled "Better Pensions for All" published by the National Liberal Federation of Canada. It says:
A new Liberal government will make it possible for all Canadians to take part in a contributory pension plan geared to growth in our economy. The plan will from the start be financially selfsupporting through contributions. It will not require any addition to taxes. As soon as the plan can be put into legislation, a minimum additional pension of $10 a month will be paid.
And, later:
As soon as the legislation is passed, and contributions start, the pension fund will be used to pay a minimum $10 a month to everyone aged 70 who would have been a contributor if he had been younger. Added to the existing old age pension this will mean pensions of $75 a month.
I also hold in my hand the pamphlet which summarizes the entire Liberal platform, entitled "The Policies of the Liberal Party", general election, 1963, published by the National Liberal Federation. It says:
To help people already retired who have not had the chance to contribute under the new Liberal plan, a minimum supplementary pension of $10 a month will be paid, from the start, out of the pension fund established by contributions. This will raise the total old age pension to $75.
The suggestion made in this house by a number of the members of the opposition that we promised there would be a $10 increase

immediately after the election, and that therefore the increase should be retroactive to April, 1963, is not true.

speechtext:
After the Liberal government took office, it moved immediately to introduce the contributory pension plan which it had promised during the election campaign. Very soon, however, Quebec announced its decision to institute its own pension plan and the premier of Ontario, while indicating his acceptance in principle of the federal plan, indicated that its implementation would require detailed study. This, of course, would necessarily result in delay.
A new situation was therefore created. With Quebec definitely out there can be no truly national contributory pension plan. If ultimately Ontario also decides to proceed with its own pension plan, it is difficult to see on what basis we can institute a federal contributory pension plan.
These circumstances, which were outside of the control of the federal government, led to the decision to split off the $10 increase from the general contributory plan. With Quebec out of the plan it would have been unfair to pay Quebec residents the $10 increase out of contributions made under the plan by the residents of other provinces. To have paid the $10 increase only to provinces which accepted the contributory plan and not to other provinces such as the province of Quebec would have caused disunity at a time when greater rather than less Canadian unity is required.

If I can gather his ideas from the welter of statistics he quoted, I understand he is making two points. The first is that the old age pension, since old age pension legislation was first introduced, has risen more rapidly than wage levels. But surely this is understandable when one realizes that old age pensions started at the miserable figure of $20 a month and have always been too low? To make a comparison between that and the increase in wage levels is a reflection on the Liberal party's viewpoint with respect to social welfare.
The second point which the hon. member was seeking to make is to the effect that putting on a tax to raise money to pay these pensions is, as he described it, an enforced redistribution of wealth. We can therefore take it that he is opposed to any type of taxation which is based on ability to pay, in order that funds might be raised to provide for those who are less fortunate than others.
This also should be made a matter of record as to where the Liberal party stands on welfare programs. As a matter of fact, far from injuring their economies, the nations which have had the most buoyant economies during the past 25 years are those that have had what the hon. member for St. Paul's calls this enforced redistribution of wealth. The table which was published by the United Nations on the standards of welfare set up by various western countries, placed Canada seventeenth on the list. It is not a very proud record; and the nations that are ahead of us, the nations that have the highest standards of health services and welfare, are all countries which have experienced a better economic growth than we have, for the very

obvious reason that their welfare programs are important economic tools for redistributing wealth and redistributing purchasing power. Far from a welfare program injuring the economy of Canada, such a program will do much to promote and stimulate the economic activity of the country.
Those who have spoken on behalf of this party have made it clear that we support this increase of $10 a month. We have been asking for it for a long time. We do not think it should have to wait until there is an election in order to persuade either of the old parties to give an increase which has been so long overdue.
We also believe that this increase in pensions should be made retroactive to April 8, for the very obvious reason that the increases to civil servants were made retroactive and that the increased indemnities to members of parliament were made retroactive to April 8. For that reason alone I do not see how the government can refuse to grant the same consideration to the old age pensioners.
As my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), pointed out the other day, we think the government should move steadily toward the goal of lowering the qualifying age for the universal old age pension to 65 years, because in industry today 65 has become the normal age at which workers retire, and there is a hiatus of five years between 65 and 70 when the average worker has no means of support unless he belongs to a private superannuation plan. Therefore by lowering the qualifying age to 65 years we would make the pension available at the normal superannuation age.
I want to say to the government that we are glad it decided to separate this increase in old age security pensions from the Canada pension plan. When the minister introduced the Canada pension plan we felt then that it was wrong to ask the old age pensioners to wait until that plan had been put into effect. We are now glad the government has separated the pension plan and the increase to old age pensioners, and that the increase is now being proceeded with.
As the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) pointed out, we are most dissatisfied with the method which the government has resorted to in order to raise the necessary funds for this increase. The hon. member for St. Paul's, who is worrying a great deal about how the money is to be raised, ought to give some consideration to what the government is planning to do. It is planning to place the entire cost of this $10 per month increase on those people who have $3,000 of taxable income or less. This means that those who have above $3,000 taxable income

will not pay any more, although their ability to pay is much greater.
I contend that if the government were willing to remove the ceiling and to apply the 3 per cent, which is now in effect, as a surcharge on all incomes, it could raise sufficient money to pay for this increase without raising the rates at all.
I am very much concerned with one statement which was made by the hon. member for St. Paul's, to the effect that if the provinces of Quebec and Ontario decided to opt out of this plan, then we cannot have a national Canada pension plan. Mr. Speaker, we did not criticize the government for changing its mind and proceeding with the $10 per month increase without waiting for the Canada pension plan. We do not criticize it, because we are glad it changed its mind, but we think we have a right to some assurance from the Minister of National Health and Welfare that this change of mind does not mean the Canada pension plan is to be dropped. We are entitled to some assurance from the minister that there will be no uncertainty about proceeding with that plan.
We know the Canada pension plan is under attack from the insurance companies of Canada. We know they are carrying on a lobby against it, a lobby of the provincial premiers and of the members of parliament. We know that speeches are being made, and literature is being disseminated, to discourage public men and women from proceeding with the Canada pension plan. Before this debate concludes the minister ought to give the house some assurance that the reason the government changed its mind, and decided to proceed with this $10 per month increase now, is merely because it did not want the old age pensioners to have to wait a number of months.
She should also assure the house that the reason is not because it is the government's intention to drop the Canada pension plan, because I disagree most strongly with the hon. member for St. Paul's and I say that if Quebec decides to have its own plan, and if the province of Ontario decides to proceed with its plan, there is no reason whatever why the other sections of Canada, which may want to proceed with a plan, should not enjoy the privileges of a national Canada pension plan.
Legislation can be drafted by which the provinces that want to opt out and conduct their own plan can do so. The Canada pension plan could apply to the remaining provinces. Within the terms of the legislation provision could be made for portability between the national plan and any provincial plans which may come into effect. But I must say I am disturbed that the hon. member

for St. Paul's may be flying a kite for the government when he suggests that if Quebec and Ontario opt out it may not be possible to have a national Canada pension plan. I hope the minister will take the opportunity in this debate to make it clear beyond any shadow of doubt that it is her intention and the government's intention to proceed with the Canada pension plan legislation so that those provinces which do not wish to opt out and are prepared to avail themselves of a universal, national pension plan will be able to do so. Once more, I repeat that the role of the opposition is to guide the government, to make suggestions and to hope that it will propose the best possible legislation, and not to constantly set a trap, to oiler amendments which only delay the implementation of legislation such as this one, which, at first sight, seems to us absolutely sound.

In my opinion, the opposition has played its role and has suggested an alternative to the government. I hope that the government will adopt the best possible policy to help our older people and that it will bring in other beneficial pieces of social legislation.
But I say nevertheless that the role of the opposition is to guide the government; and if the government brings in other similar social measures, which will benefit all Canadians, it is with pleasure that we shall support those measures.

I believe the deletion of the entire clause is necessary because two or three alterations are proposed and the amendment reads with greater clarity if that is done. It continues:
2. Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. minister but it seems to me that before going into the essence of the proposal

put forward by the hon. member for Skeena the Chair should be given an opportunity to rule on the validity of the amendment.
In the very few minutes I have had at my disposal since this amendment has been proposed to the committee I have looked up certain authorities and I should like to make the following ruling: This amendment is out of order for the reason that it seeks to introduce a new proposal which is outside the scope of the bill as it was approved earlier today on second reading. It is, therefore, irrelevant and I should like to quote from May's Parliamentary Practice, sixteenth edition at page 421, where it says:
Stated generally, no matter ought to be raised in debate on a question which would be irrelevant if moved as an amendment, and an amendment cannot be used for importing arguments which would be irrelevant to the main question.
The proposal put forward by the hon. member is one which would have the effect of negating an essential principle of the bill as approved on second reading.
I submit, also, that it is out of order because it seeks to change the incidence of the tax as implied in the bill. I should like to refer hon. members to Beauchesne, fourth edition, paragraph 276 where it is stated:
In early editions of this book (Sir T. Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice), it was stated that "the crown has no concern in the distribution of taxes." Hence amendments were at first permitted which proposed the substitution of a different tax for a tax proposed by the government (provided that both were estimated to yield an equivalent amount) on the ground that the necessity of next taxation to that extent had already been declared on behalf of the crown. In modern practice this view is regarded as incomplete, and so requiring to be, supplemented by the view that the royal initiation in taxation implies the exclusive right to define the incidence as well as the amount of burdens to be placed upon the people, and that an amendment which transfers a burden to taxpayers not previously liable is an infringement on this initiative.
The motion by which a tax is proposed in committee of ways and means is now treated as an effective expression of the financial initiative of the crown, and therefore as the standard in relation to which the admissibility of amendments is determined. Accordingly an amendment is debarred, not only from increasing the rate of a tax, but also from extending its incidence to new classes, even while proposing to relieve other classes of payers.
For these reasons I declare, with regret, that the proposed amendment is out of order.

The reasons given this afternoon by the Minister of Finance for not doing so were, it seemed to me,
Old Age Security
flimsy. The first ground for refusal was, as I recall it, that if we intend to revise personal income taxes this is not the time to do it. Well, of course, it is never the time to do it. The fact is that we are now proposing taxation which is not equitable, taxation which is not levied on the basis of ability to pay. The hon. gentleman says some other time would be the time at which to do what we are asking, which means it will never be done. If the committee intends to deal with this question it should deal with it now.
The other objection the Minister of Finance had was that those in the upper income brackets would be paying a great deal more than the rest, but they would not be eligible for any greater benefits and that we would therefore be taxing them in respect of benefits they were not going to get. I submit that this is precisely what we are doing now, only with respect to people in the lower income brackets. For instance, a man who all his life never earns more than $2,000 or $2,500 a year may never pay this tax, yet he will naturally draw a full pension. Surely, the whole principle of taxation is "From each according to his ability to pay and to each according to his needs". That is the principle of all welfare legislation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext: We pay our taxes on the basis of ability to pay and the return we get is not necessarily commensurate with what we have contributed. No one has ever suggested that this is an insurance plan. It is an old age security measure which entitles people to a certain income at a certain age irrespective of whether they have contributed anything to the fund or not. The return which a senior citizen is entitled to receive has nothing to do with what the citizen may have paid in over a period of years. Therefore it is beside the point to suggest that if the ceiling is removed a taxpayer with $10,000 or $12,000 taxable income will be paying more without getting any larger return when he is eligible. It seems to me that on the basis of good welfare legislation-not insurance legislation but good welfare legislation-the proper thing to do is to say that the payments will be levied on the basis of ability to pay on the entire taxable income. If this were done it would remove the necessity of increasing the rate from 3 per cent to 4 per cent. I certainly believe that the government should give very serious consideration to this point because I think the people of Canada would recognize the equity in the proposal we have made.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. I hope the hon. gentleman will not feel that there is any departure from proper procedure but the Prime Minister did indicate some time ago that if the effort to establish a private trusteeship was not successful the house would be asked to proceed immediately with the first stage of that legislation, which is the resolution now on the order paper. That, therefore, will be the first item of business for tomorrow. As tomorrow is a Wednesday I suppose it will probably be the only item of business, but should it be concluded we would then proceed with the program which was uncompleted today, that is to say the Northwest Territories bill and the bill for the other territory, and the vocational training measure.
It being ten minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Wednesday, October 9, 1963
